lines: Thunder shook the smithing table hard enough to make every loose tool dance.
I checked the handles after the lightning, then counted heads.
The bell sounded small under that thunder. We stayed inside and watched the doors.
That last crack made everyone jump at once.
The sky can keep its lightning. I have enough sparks in the shop.
A roof tile landed beside my grindstone. A little closer and I would need a new one.
I covered the coal and moved everyone away from the windows.
The iron rang on the wall every time the thunder rolled.
I found three children under my workbench. They chose a sturdy hiding place.
We moved away from the windows when the clouds turned green.
Lightning split the old fence post by the well.
Rain came through the chimney and put half my coals out.
The storm passed, but my ears are still waiting for the next crack.
I checked the weather vane afterward. It is pointing down now.
No one was struck. That matters more than the tools knocked off the wall.
The golem stood in the rain like thunder was none of its business.
I kept a hammer close, though I have no idea what good it does against weather.
We will need nails for the shutters once the wind settles.
The youngest villagers counted the seconds after every flash.
Everything is damp, loud, and still standing. I will take it.
I checked the wooden handles and coal dust for sparks first.
We passed water hand to hand and kept people away from the smoke.
The tools can wait. People come first.
We saved what we could reach, then stopped risking lives for belongings.
The smoke is thinning, but everyone is still sniffing the air.
One bucket line reached from the well clear to the workshop.
I threw every oily rag outside before the flames reached this end of the street.
The heat warped two saw blades hanging on the wall.
A farmer kicked in the back door to make sure no one was trapped.
We found the missing child under a wet blanket by the fountain.
My hands smell like soot no matter how much I scrub them.
The roof beam held long enough for us to clear the room.
Someone saved the order book. I would rather they had saved their eyebrows.
We need to watch the ashes until morning.
Half the village is coughing, but everyone answered the count.
I can replace burned handles. I cannot replace a neighbor.
The water ruined a few tools. Good. Water was where it needed to be.
We rolled the coal sacks outside before the flames reached them.
Tomorrow we rebuild. Tonight we make sure no ember starts again.
The fire is out. Keep the lane clear for anyone carrying water.
During a raid, the tools can wait. Who gets behind a door matters more.
The horns stopped, but my hands still expect another wave from the road.
We counted living neighbors before tools and repairs.
<red><bold>Raiders</bold></red> came looking for easy emeralds. They found barred doors and stubborn people.
From the workshop I saw fear cross the square, then courage get there first.
I handed out every axe that could hold an edge.
The grindstone ran until the first horn sounded.
One raider tried the workshop door. The new hinges held.
We used tool crates to block the narrow lane.
The bell rope snapped halfway through. Someone kept ringing it by hand.
I saw the golem take a crossbow bolt and keep walking.
Two picks came back chipped. Their owners came back alive.
The last raider fled past the fields just before dawn.
I have never been happier to hear villagers arguing over the damage.
We will repair the doors after everyone has been treated.
My best hammer is missing. I hope whoever grabbed it needed it.
The square is quiet now, but nobody trusts the silence.
I spent the fight fitting spare handles onto whatever people brought me.
We held because everyone did one useful thing at the right time.
The raid is over. Keep watch until the scouts return.
Night trouble tested the loose latch by the workshop first.
I stayed by the tool rack and listened for anyone calling from the dark.
At dawn, the tools stayed put while I helped count the wounded.
The dark tested everyone. Most of us held together.
We are safe enough, though every shadow is being checked twice.
Something scratched at the shutters until the golem reached it.
I gave the night watch a lantern and my heaviest hammer.
Nobody slept after the first scream from the edge of the village.
We moved the children into the stone house before the second alarm.
An arrow came through the workshop window and buried itself in the rack.
The moon made every fence post look like a pillager.
I heard fighting by the well but could not see who was there.
Dawn showed us how close the attackers came to the beds.
One door bar cracked. I am making three replacements today.
We kept the lamps low so the watch could see beyond the walls.
The old shovel by the door has a new dent and no one will admit using it.
We found tracks circling the houses after sunrise.
Tonight every latch gets checked before the sun goes down.
No one should walk to the fields alone until we know what attacked us.
The night ended. My hands have not stopped shaking yet.
The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still cleaning grit from the hinges.
I checked who was coughing before I checked the tools.
Sand reached the workbench and half our eyes, but no one is missing.
A hard wind shows which doors close and which only pretend.
The whole village sounds like it is chewing gravel.
I wrapped the grindstone before the grit could ruin it.
We tied a rope between the workshop and the well so nobody lost the path.
The sky disappeared before the last villager made it indoors.
Sand packed the doorframe so tightly we had to dig our way out.
I found a dune where my coal pile used to be.
Every moving part in the shop needs cleaning now.
A child followed the rope home with both eyes shut.
The wind took three roof tiles and returned somebody else's bucket.
We stuffed cloth under the doors and still tasted dust all night.
I am checking water jars for grit before anyone drinks.
The storm polished one side of every sign in the village.
Visibility dropped so fast the bell became our only landmark.
My files are wrapped and my lungs wish they had been.
The worst has passed. Cover your face until the air clears.
We came through with sore eyes and a great deal of sweeping ahead.
The tools can wait. Warm hands and clear paths come first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone found shelter.
Cold works quietly. We are checking on anyone who stayed quiet too long.
I am clearing ice off the shovel blades and watching for lost tracks.
We are alright for now. Keep the fires fed and the paths open.
The workshop roof groaned under the snow before dawn.
I fitted fresh handles to every shovel we could find.
A drift buried the lane between here and the bakery.
We tied bright cloth to the doors so people could find them in the whiteout.
The cold made the iron painful to touch without gloves.
Someone brought hot soup to the night watch. That helped more than another shovel.
I found ice inside a closed tool chest. I am still working that out.
The bell froze until we warmed it with a lantern.
We took turns clearing the same path every hour.
No one goes outside alone until the wind drops.
The chimney draw is poor in this weather. Check rooms for smoke.
A farmer's roof sagged, so half the village went up with poles.
My boots are wet through and there is still another doorway to clear.
The snow has stopped. The cold has not.
Count every bed tonight. A missing neighbor cannot wait until morning.
